newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian town turns lawless after police flee.
newsitem.headline: Albanian town turns lawless after police flee.

text.p: Ever since an angry crowd of anti-government protesters chased off local police with a hail of stones, this southern Albanian port town has become an Eldorado for gangs, small-time criminals and smugglers.
After dark, only a handful of youths dare to walk along the dusty sidewalk of Vlore's main boulevard, where rows of palm trees barely hide crumbling Soviet-style apartment buildings.
The scores of makeshift cafes and gambling halls along the potholed street are now practically empty.
"People are too scared at night," says Skender, 35. "Anything can happen these days".
Vlore is slowly descending into criminal anarchy that has prompted even opposition parties, gearing up for a 10th day of street protests, to ask authorities for police reinforcements.
"We need to bring back law and order," a local leader of the opposition Social Democrats told Reuters.
Earlier this week the dilapidated town was the scene of some of the worst unrest in Albania since 40 years of Stalinism fell in the small Balkan nation six years ago.
Violence was sparked by the collapse of a local investment scheme with some $500 million in debt, leaving the majority of the town's 90,000 inhabitants penniless.
Local police abandoned the city when an angry mob stoned a group of riot policemen, stripped them and burnt their clothes and gear in a bonfire.
A new police chief was installed on Tuesday, but security forces are keeping a low profile and uniform police are nowhere to be seen.
Incidents of random violence and lawlessness have risen, sending fear through the town's residents.

Three masked gunmen broke into Hamid Dule's apartment on Wednesday and abducted his 18-year-old daughter. Dule was shot three times. Locals say his daughter has been taken across the Adriatic and will be forced to work as a prostitute in Italy.
Just hours before, a policeman was shot dead in a suburb of Vlore in what authorities said was a gangland killing prompted by a bloody vendetta between two local families.
Vlore's biggest exports, drugs and illegal emigrants, have staged a new boom ever since security was relaxed.

"Now we are in charge. This is the perfect moment to smuggle clandestini (illegal emigrants) to neighbouring Italy," says Besnik, a 35-year-old speedboat owner. "Police are nowhere and you can do your job without any problems."
Besnik says he and his colleagues normally charge $500 per passage for Albanians. Kurds and Asians have to pay a little more -- "$700 for me and $300 for the middleman," he explained.
"Yesterday I transported 25 clandestinis of whom 10 were left penniless by the collapse of several pyramid schemes," he said.

The destitute investors, who once believed becoming rich meant little more than sitting around in a cafe and waiting for money to double, blame the right-wing government of President Sali Berisha for their plight.
They want their money back, saying the government should have stopped the private schemes, and they want the government to quit.
"We have to topple this government at any cost," says Besnik. "In the five years of Berisha's rule, we have seen nothing but theft, vandalism and unemployment."
